subject: ela
skillName: Develop and strengthen writing through planning, revising, editing
intro: Strong writing is built in stages. First you plan by gathering and grouping ideas. Then you draft. Then you revise to improve the ideas, focus, and organization, and you edit to fix surface conventions like spelling, capitalization, and punctuation. When a draft still does not work after small fixes, the best move is often to rewrite a section or try a new approach. The key difference to keep clear is that revising changes content and structure, while editing only corrects conventions without changing meaning.

items.prompt: Read the described action: 'Before writing her report, Dana lists every fact she knows about volcanoes, then circles the three facts she wants to use and numbers them in the order she will write them.' Which stage of the writing process is Dana in: planning, revising, editing, or publishing?

steps: Look at what Dana is doing and when she is doing it. She is working before she writes the report.
She lists ideas, then chooses and orders the ones she wants. Gathering, grouping, and ordering ideas before drafting is the work of planning (prewriting).
It is not revising or editing, because those stages happen after a draft exists. It is not publishing, because she has not finished or shared anything.
So Dana is in the planning stage.
solution.answer: Planning. She is gathering, choosing, and ordering ideas before she drafts, which is the work of the planning stage.

items.prompt: A writer made this change to a draft: 'She moved the last sentence of her paragraph to the very beginning so the main idea comes first.' Is this change revising or editing? Explain how you know.

steps: Decide what the change affects. Moving a sentence changes the order and structure of the paragraph.
Revising means changing ideas, content, or organization to make the writing stronger. Editing means correcting surface conventions like spelling and punctuation without changing meaning.
Reordering sentences to put the main idea first improves organization, so it is revising, not editing.
This change does not fix a spelling, capitalization, or punctuation error, which confirms it is revising.
solution.answer: Revising. Reordering sentences to improve organization changes the structure of the writing, which is a revising task, not a surface-level edit.

items.prompt: Read this sentence from a draft: 'The storm was very bad and the storm made the trees move a lot.' Which revision most improves the sentence: (A) 'The storm was bad and made the trees move a lot.' (B) 'The fierce storm whipped the trees back and forth.' (C) 'The storm, which was very bad, moved the trees.' (D) 'The storm was very, very bad for the trees.'?

steps: Find the problems in the original. It repeats 'the storm' and uses vague words like 'very bad' and 'move a lot.'
A strong revision should replace vague, repeated words with precise language and combine the ideas smoothly.
Choice B replaces 'very bad' with 'fierce' and 'made the trees move a lot' with 'whipped the trees back and forth,' and it removes the repetition. That is precise and clear.
Choice A still uses vague wording. Choice C is wordy and keeps 'very bad.' Choice D just repeats 'very' and stays vague.
So choice B is the strongest revision.
solution.answer: Choice B: 'The fierce storm whipped the trees back and forth.' It removes the repeated words and replaces vague language with precise verbs and adjectives.

items.prompt: Read this paragraph: 'Our school should start a recycling club. A recycling club would have many benefits. My favorite color is green. Students could collect paper and cans and keep them out of the trash.' During revision, which sentence should be cut because it does not belong, and why?

steps: Identify the topic of the paragraph. It is about why the school should start a recycling club.
Check each sentence against that topic. The first, second, and fourth sentences all support the recycling club idea.
The sentence 'My favorite color is green' is about a personal preference, not the recycling club. It is off topic.
During revision, off-topic details should be cut so the paragraph stays focused. So that sentence should be removed.
solution.answer: Cut 'My favorite color is green.' It is off topic and does not support the paragraph's main idea about starting a recycling club.

items.prompt: Read this sentence with errors: 'me and my brother walks to the libary on tuesday.' Choose the edited version that corrects the conventions without changing the meaning: (A) 'Me and my brother walks to the library on Tuesday.' (B) 'My brother and I walk to the library on Tuesday.' (C) 'My brother and I walk to the libary on tuesday.' (D) 'My brother and I walked to a store on Tuesday.'?

steps: List the convention errors: 'me' should be the subject pronoun 'I,' the verb should agree as 'walk,' 'libary' is misspelled, and 'Tuesday' needs a capital T. The sentence should also start with a capital letter.
Choice B fixes the pronoun to 'My brother and I,' corrects the verb to 'walk,' spells 'library' correctly, and capitalizes 'Tuesday.'
Choice A still uses 'Me' and 'walks.' Choice C keeps 'libary' and 'tuesday' wrong. Choice D changes the meaning by switching 'library' to 'store' and 'walk' to 'walked.'
Editing must fix conventions without changing meaning, so choice B is correct.
solution.answer: Choice B: 'My brother and I walk to the library on Tuesday.' It corrects the pronoun, verb agreement, spelling, and capitalization while keeping the original meaning.

items.prompt: Read the described action: 'After finishing his whole essay, Marcus reads it once more and fixes three spelling mistakes and adds a missing period.' Which stage of the writing process is Marcus in: planning, revising, editing, or publishing?
items.hint: Ask whether the change fixes surface conventions like spelling and punctuation, or whether it changes the ideas and organization.

steps: Marcus is working after the essay is finished, and he is fixing spelling and a missing period.
Correcting spelling and punctuation are surface conventions, which is the work of editing.
He is not adding ideas or changing organization, so it is not revising or planning, and he has not shared the work, so it is not publishing.
So Marcus is in the editing stage.
solution.answer: Editing. Fixing spelling and punctuation corrects surface conventions, which is the work of the editing stage.

items.prompt: Read this sentence from a draft: 'The food at the party was good and the food tasted good too.' Which revision most improves it: (A) 'The food at the party was good and tasted good.' (B) 'The food at the party was fresh and full of flavor.' (C) 'The food, which was good, tasted good at the party.' (D) 'The good food at the party was really good.'?
items.hint: Look for repeated, vague words like 'good.' The best revision replaces them with precise language instead of repeating the idea.

steps: The original repeats 'good' and the idea that the food tasted good. The words are vague.
A strong revision replaces vague, repeated words with precise language.
Choice B uses precise words, 'fresh' and 'full of flavor,' and removes the repetition.
Choices A, C, and D all keep the vague word 'good' or repeat the idea, so they do not improve clarity.
solution.answer: Choice B: 'The food at the party was fresh and full of flavor.' It replaces the repeated, vague word 'good' with precise description.

items.prompt: Read this paragraph: 'Dogs make great pets. They are loyal and can be trained to follow rules. Cats are also nice animals. A dog will greet its owner happily every day.' During revision, which sentence should be cut because it does not belong, and why?
items.hint: Decide what the paragraph is mainly about, then find the sentence that drifts to a different subject.

steps: The paragraph's main idea is that dogs make great pets.
Sentences one, two, and four all support why dogs are great pets.
The sentence 'Cats are also nice animals' shifts to a different topic, cats, and does not support the point about dogs.
During revision, that off-topic sentence should be removed so the paragraph stays focused on dogs.
solution.answer: Cut 'Cats are also nice animals.' It shifts to a different topic and does not support the main idea that dogs make great pets.

items.prompt: A writer has a confusing paragraph that readers cannot follow. Twice she has tried to fix it by swapping a single word each time, but readers are still lost. What should she do next: (A) swap one more word and hope it works, (B) rewrite the paragraph and try a new approach, (C) fix a spelling error in it, or (D) add a comma somewhere in it?
items.hint: If small word changes have already failed twice, the problem is probably bigger than one word.

steps: The paragraph is confusing as a whole, and small word fixes have already failed twice.
When a draft still does not work after small fixes, the strongest move is to rewrite the section or try a new approach.
Choice B rewrites and tries a new approach, which addresses the real problem.
Choices A, C, and D are all small surface fixes that will not solve a paragraph readers cannot follow.
solution.answer: Choice B: rewrite the paragraph and try a new approach. Small word fixes have already failed, so the draft needs a bigger change.

items.prompt: Read this sentence with errors: 'the kids was excited becuase the show started on friday.' Choose the edited version that corrects the conventions without changing the meaning: (A) 'The kids were excited because the show started on Friday.' (B) 'the kids were excited becuase the show started on friday.' (C) 'The kids was excited because the show started on Friday.' (D) 'The kids were thrilled because the movie started on Friday.'?
items.hint: Find every surface error first: capitalization, subject-verb agreement, spelling. The right answer fixes them all without changing any words' meaning.

steps: List the errors: the sentence needs a capital 'The,' the verb should be 'were' to agree with 'kids,' 'becuase' is misspelled, and 'Friday' needs a capital F.
Choice A capitalizes 'The,' uses 'were,' spells 'because' correctly, and capitalizes 'Friday.'
Choice B keeps lowercase and the misspelling. Choice C keeps 'was,' which does not agree with 'kids.'
Choice D changes meaning by switching 'excited' to 'thrilled' and 'show' to 'movie,' so it is not a clean edit.
Choice A is the correct edit.
solution.answer: Choice A: 'The kids were excited because the show started on Friday.' It fixes capitalization, verb agreement, and spelling while keeping the original meaning.
